title: "fatal: bad object" — repairing a damaged repository
summary: Corrupt the index, then a loose object, and repair both. Learn which parts of .git are disposable, which are precious, and how content-addressing makes most damage detectable.
mental_model: Every object's filename is the hash of its content, so any corruption is detectable — git recomputes the hash and complains. The index, the reflog and packfiles are caches that can be rebuilt; the objects and refs are the only irreplaceable parts.
danger: Never delete files under .git/objects to 'clean up'. Every one of them is content that nothing else can reproduce.

steps.title: Check the repository is healthy first
steps.why: `fsck` verifies that every object's content still hashes to its name and that every ref points at something real. Run it before you believe any diagnosis.
steps.expect: No output from fsck beyond progress — silence means healthy.

steps.title: Destroy the index
steps.why: `.git/index` is a cache of the staging area. Corrupting it breaks `status` and `add` immediately, which looks catastrophic and is not.
steps.expect: fatal: index file smaller than expected, or a similar refusal.

steps.title: Rebuild it from HEAD
steps.why: Deleting the index and running `git reset` regenerates it from the commit. You lose only what was staged and uncommitted — everything else was never in the index to begin with.
steps.expect: Status works again, tree clean, history untouched.

verify.label: the index was rebuilt from HEAD

steps.title: Now corrupt a real object
steps.why: Loose objects live at `.git/objects/ab/cdef...`. Overwriting one breaks the content-addressing invariant — and because the filename IS the hash, git can prove something is wrong rather than silently serving bad data.

actions.run: sh -c 'sha=$(git rev-parse HEAD~1); dir=.git/objects/${sha%${sha#??}}; file=.git/objects/${sha:0:2}/${sha:2}; chmod u+w "$file" 2>/dev/null; printf "corrupted" > "$file"; echo damaged $file'

steps.expect: fsck reports a corrupt or invalid object, naming the sha.

steps.title: Fetch the missing object back from a clone
steps.why: Git is distributed, which is a backup strategy as well as a workflow. Any clone has the same objects under the same names, so copying one back repairs the damage exactly.

actions.run: sh -c 'sha=$(git rev-parse HEAD~1 2>/dev/null || echo ""); echo repairing from origin'
sh -c 'cd ../origin.git && git cat-file -p HEAD >/dev/null && echo origin healthy'

commands: sh -c 'cd ../origin.git && git fsck --full && echo "origin is intact"'
steps.expect: The origin repository is undamaged and has the object you lost.

steps.title: Repair by re-cloning and moving your work across
steps.why: For a single missing object you can copy the file from another clone. When several are damaged, the honest fix is a fresh clone plus re-applying whatever was only local — which is why 'commit and push often' is a durability practice, not just a collaboration one.
steps.expect: A healthy repository containing everything that was pushed.

verify.label: …and contains everything that had been pushed

steps.title: Notice exactly what was lost
steps.why: The 'Add alerts' commit was never pushed, so no clone has it. That is the real lesson of this scenario: the only work at risk from local corruption is the work that exists in exactly one place.
steps.expect: Two commits — the unpushed third is gone with the damaged repository.

verify.label: the unpushed commit could not be recovered from anywhere else
you ended with a healthy repository
verify.hint: re-clone from a remote that still has the objects

verify.label: everything that had been pushed was recovered
the unpushed commit was genuinely lost — the point of the exercise
the origin repository was never damaged

pitfalls: The index, reflogs and packfiles are caches. `.git/objects` and `.git/refs` are not — never delete anything there.
`rm .git/index && git reset` fixes almost every 'index is corrupt' error, and costs you only staged-but-uncommitted work.
A corrupt object in a packfile is harder: `git unpack-objects` from a healthy clone's pack, or just re-clone.
`git fsck --full` on a huge repository is slow but reads everything. Run it before concluding a repository is fine.
Work that exists only on your laptop has no backup. Pushing a branch — even a scruffy one — is the cheapest durability you will ever get.
cheatsheet: pack loose objects, prune unreachable ones
the most reliable repair of all
